title: Nekuda, sefira, partzuf: why the essential points of Tohu break, and how Tikun makes a person
overview:
Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus*, the chapter brings in *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*: the difference between *Tohu* and *Tikun*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is a point, the essence of an attribute before it spreads: a will for kindness that has a definition but no reason and no particular ways, like a person who is kind by nature, not one who read Dale Carnegie. Even its intellect and its *netzach* are the same point, all in one vessel, the *Akudim*.

So the *sefiros* of *Tohu* cannot join: two opposite essential goals allow no compromise, and whoever makes one of them the cure-all, "totally nice, always" or "get it yourself", fails. *Tikun* is the will for how to reach the goal. Kindness then depends on a reason, and one thing can be loved and hated at once, as G-d punished Shaul and ordered his eulogy at the same time. Only *Tikun* makes a *partzuf*, a person who sees the goal both sides share and takes the practical step, the way G-d mixed fire and water.

terms.gloss: the world of Chaos: each sefira only a point, an essential goal that cannot join its opposite
the world of Repair: each sefira divided into ten, so that they work together in harmony; the will for how to reach the goal
a point: the essence of an attribute before it spreads out, a bias with no reason and no particular ways
inclusion: the attributes working together like a harmony
the Name of forty-five: the abstract that a concrete form, BaN, comes to express
the Name of fifty-two: the concrete form, a vessel or an angel, that represents the abstract MaH
the bound ones: all ten sefiros included in one vessel, all one point
here: the point of Tohu even when divided into ten, each still a point, with no inclusion
lit. face: the stature of a person, the inclusion of all opposites; only in Tikun
composite kindness: kindness that depends on a reason, such as to one who did you a favor, weighed out by the situation
a middle: the place a thing loved from one side and hated from another ends up on one's list
a person of daas, who explains each of two opposite views better than its holder and finds the goal they share

sections.title: Before the sefiros of Atzilus: nekuda, sefira, partzuf, and the difference between Tohu and Tikun
sections.summary: Before the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus* are explained one by one, the chapter brings in the three stages *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*. In *Tohu* each *sefira* is only a point; in *Tikun* each is divided into ten, and so they work together in harmony, through the Name *MaH*.

phrases.he: (כ) והנה קודם שיבואר ענין פרטי העשר ספירות דאצילות יש להקדים ענין נקודה ספירה פרצוף כו'
דהיות ידוע ההפרש שבין בחינת התהו לבחינת התיקון בכלל,
דעשר ספירות דתהו הן בבחינת נקודות לבד,
phrases.en: In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*.

phrases.he: שהן בבחינת הכתרים

blocks.text: Now he starts on *Keser* (crown). First the chapter explains *nekudos*, *sefira* and *partzuf* (points, a single attribute, and a full stature of attributes), and *Tikun* and *Tohu* (the worlds of Repair and of Chaos), to show how the *igulim* (circles) of *Atzilus* relate to its *yosher* (the straight line).

**In *Tohu*, each *sefira* is like a *nekuda*** (a point), not yet ten. As the last chapter explained, tying your *etzem ratzon* (essential will) to something makes a bias, a leaning towards *chesed* (kindness) or another way. The leaning is only a point, not yet a particular will for anything, but it is the general source of every particular that comes out after.

phrases.he: ובעולם התיקון הוא בבחינת התחלקות כל ספירה לי',
phrases.en: And then in *Tikun*, each *sefira* becomes already divided to ten.

phrases.he: על כן ממילא נעשה בחינת התיקון
phrases.en: and since each *sefira* is now diverse, it automatically makes it *Tikun*.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות
phrases.en: That's the idea of *hiskalelus*, that it's like a harmony.

phrases.he: על ידי שם מ''ה כו'

blocks.text: In *Tikun* each *sefira* is already divided into ten, and because each is now diverse, that automatically makes it *Tikun*. *Tikun* has many senses; here it means a harmony, the things working together. That is *hiskalelus* (inclusion): **it's like a harmony**.

The harmony comes through the Name *MaH* (the Name of forty-five). *MaH* and *BaN* always relate the same way: when something concrete with a set form, a *kli* (vessel) or an angel, can carry something abstract, the abstract is *MaH* and the *kli* *BaN*.

blocks.title: Letters make a vessel for an idea
blocks.text: Language, for example: words are a tangible form, but arranging letters in different orders makes a *kli* that can express an abstract idea.

sections.title: The point: the essence of a midda before it spreads, a will for kindness with no reason
sections.summary: The *nekuda* is the essence of an attribute before it spreads out. It is not the essence as it is in the *yechida*, but the will for kindness once it is revealed: it already has a definition, but no reason and no particular ways of coming out.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים ידוע שבחינת הנקודות הוא בחינת העצמיות טרם שמתפשט,
phrases.en: The *nekudos* is like the *etzem* before it spreads out,

phrases.he: כנקודה שהיא בלתי מתפשטת כו'
phrases.en: like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet.

blocks.text: The *nekudos* are the *etzem* (essence) before it spreads out. As the *igulim* are the soul before it enters the body and the *yosher* the soul entering it, so *Tohu* and *Tikun* are the thing in its *etzem* and the thing coming out, the *hispashtus* (spreading forth). The point is **like a *nekuda* that doesn't come out yet**, still in its *etzem hiyuli* (the raw, formless essence).

phrases.he: כמו אור מדת החסד,
phrases.en: for example, *chesed*,

phrases.he: הנה בחינת עצמיות דמדת החסד הוא בחינת הכתר שלו

blocks.text: Take, **for example, *chesed***: the essence of the attribute is its *Keser*. The *etzem* of the *midda* (attribute) of kindness is a desire for kindness, so that a person always leans towards doing things nicely.

phrases.he: ואמנם אין הכוונה על בחינת העצמיות דמדת החסד כמו שהוא נטוע ומושרש בעצם הנפש שנקרא יחידה
phrases.en: But we're not talking here about the *etzem* like it is in the *yechida*,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל, שהוא בחינת היולי לגמרי (כנזכר לעיל באות יו''ד וי''א)
אלא הכוונה הוא על בחינת גלוי הרצון לדבר חסד פרטי
phrases.en: We're talking about now when a person has a particular *ratzon* for doing an actual kind thing.

phrases.he: מן העלם חסד העצמיות ההיולי

blocks.text: This is not the essence of *chesed* as it is rooted in the essence of the soul, the *yechida*, where it is wholly *hiyuli* (raw potential); that is before the *tzimtzum* (contraction), as chapters 10 and 11 said.

It is the will for a particular act of *chesed*, revealed out of the hidden kindness of the essence. The essential *chesed* made a *ratzon* (will) to be a nice person; *Adam Kadmon* makes it a picture of what a nice person is; and the picture now yields particular *ratzonos* (wills) to do nice things.

Yet all those kind acts still share one *nekuda*, that he sees them as nice: the essence carries over into them. Through *Adam Kadmon*, *chesed* now has a definition you could look up in a dictionary, but the point, wanting whatever is nice, is still there.

phrases.he: שגם זה הרצון
phrases.en: even this particular *ratzon*, that you want to do a nice thing,

phrases.he: הוא בלתי התפשטות עדיין
רק כמו שהוא בלא טעם כלל
phrases.en: this is without any reason at all,

phrases.he: לרצון זה, למה רוצה בגלוי לחסד זה כו'
ומכל שכן שאין בו בחינת התחלקות אופנים שונים
phrases.en: and he definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do.

blocks.text: Even this will to do nice things is still without *hispashtus*. He knows what being nice means, but has nothing particular yet; the situation will decide what comes out. Like a nice person: he leans towards kindness, but right now nothing is coming up, so he is not doing anything.
And **this is without any reason at all**. He does not want it to reach some goal in a given situation; the *chesed* is the goal. That is his *etzem*, the *nekuda*: he likes it because of who he is.

blocks.title: Dale Carnegie's book
blocks.text: It is not like someone who is nice to people because he read Dale Carnegie's *How to Win Friends and Influence People* and knows a career needs it. Being nice is not that person's *ratzon*; the *nekuda* of his will is to make money, or whatever it may be.

But a person whose nature is *chafetz chesed* (desires kindness) builds a self-image as a kind person, and being kind is his goal in life, or part of it. Such an *Adam Kadmon* gives him a constant *nekuda*: he wants to do kind things.

Still less is it divided into separate ways. Since it is no means to an end, he **definitely didn't yet think up particular ways of exactly what he wants to do**: no will for this or that, only for whatever will be kind.

blocks.title: A will for money, from any deal
blocks.text: Likewise someone with an *etzem ratzon* for money does not care how it comes, from this deal or that; he just wants the money. So too here: he wants the *chesed*, and does not care how it comes out.

sections.title: Intellect and victory inside the point: all one point, the Akudim in one vessel
sections.summary: Even the bias of the intellect towards kindness, the *chachma* of that *chesed*, and its *netzach* are only the same point. The ten are there, but with no recognizable division: this is the world of *Akudim*, all in one *kli*.

phrases.he: או גם אם שכלו מטה כלפי חסד דווקא, אין בו התחלקות אופנים שונים
אף על פי ששכל הנוטה בעצם לחסד ולזכות, הוא בחינת חכמה שבחסד העצמי, אבל גם הוא רק בבחינת נקודה

blocks.question: If his essential will biases his intellect towards kindness, is that not *chachma*, a division already within the point?
blocks.text: That too is a *nekuda*, not an actual *sechel* (intellect) yet. His *sechel* will always lean to being liberal and kind, to looking at things with a good eye; but the leaning is part of the same point, with no division into different ways.

His intellect leaning to kindness and merit is the *chachma* (wisdom) of the essential *chesed*, but only as a point. Everything, even in *Tohu*, divides ten within ten, so a *chachma* is there; but it is the same *nekuda*: his *chachma* and his *middos* (emotional attributes) all want *chesed*. It is a point because it is not yet about any situation; whatever comes up, he already leans this way.

phrases.he: וכן נצח שבחסד זה
phrases.en: that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed*.

phrases.he: הוא בא בבחינת נקודה
ונמצא דגם שבחינת החסד העצמי הבא בגלוי כלול מי', רצון ושכל ומדות, אבל אין בהם התחלקות ניכרת
phrases.en: even though really, technically, it does have ten, you could divide it up into ten *sefiros*, there's no recognizable distinction

phrases.he: אלא כולן בבחינת נקודה אחד,
phrases.en: they're all in one *nekuda*,

phrases.he: והוא בחינת העקודים, שעקודים היו בכלי אחד כו'
phrases.en: This is the level of *Akudim*, where really all of the ten *sefiros* are included in one *kli*,

blocks.text: So too the *netzach* (victory) of this *chesed*: **that he's going to want to overcome any opposition to any *chesed***. Nothing stands in his way yet, but if something did, he would fight it. This too comes as a point.

So the essential *chesed* coming into the open includes all ten, will, intellect and *middos*, with no recognizable division. You could technically divide it into ten *sefiros*, but they are one *nekuda*: everything together goes to *chesed*.

Rather, **they're all in one *nekuda***. **This is the level of *Akudim***, the bound ones: all ten *sefiros* in one *kli*. His *ratzon*, *sechel* and *middos* now mean one thing, that he wants *chesed*, and it does not matter which you name. It is simply his final goal.

sections.title: Sefira: the sefiros of Tohu cannot join, and two opposite goals cannot compromise
sections.summary: Because each *sefira* of *Tohu* is an essential goal, they cannot unite: one reigns and dies, then the next. Two opposite essential wills cannot be mixed or compromised, and a person or a society that makes one of them the cure-all fails; so too Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel could not convince each other.

phrases.he: ולזה בחינת עשר ספירות דתהו הן בלתי מתיחדין ומתכללין זה עם זה
phrases.en: And therefore the *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include with each other at all,

phrases.he: אלא הן זה תחת זה
phrases.en: they're one under the other,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב וימלוך וימת כו'

blocks.text: So the ten *sefiros* of *Tohu* do not unite or include each other at all. They are one below the other, as it says of each king of *Tohu*, "and he reigned, and he died": the kings of Esav, who stand for the kings of *Tohu*.

phrases.he: כמו רצון העצמי שבא בגלוי חסד
הגם שכלול בו שכל כו', לא יתחבר עם רצון עצמי היפוכו הבא בבחינת הדין

blocks.text: So the essential will that comes out as *chesed*, intellect and all, will not join the opposite essential will, which comes as *din* (judgement). You see it very much in politics: for whatever reason, one person leans liberal, another conservative.
You see it in anything people believe in, as with missionaries and the like: it is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to, and they believe it whatever it is.

sensitivity.reason: Holds up missionaries as the type of believer whose reasoning is only a front for a fixed belief.
sensitivity.publishable: You see it in anything people believe in: it is really a belief, an *etzem nekuda* they are connected to, and they believe it whatever it is.

blocks.text: So both sides come into *sechel* to convince you, but it is not really *sechel*; it is *ratzon*, still their belief. You could argue with such a person forever and never convince him, because his *sechel* runs one way: "*sechel*'s a puppet to convince you of what they believe."

That is not necessarily bad; this is how it starts. At this level that is what *sechel* is for: to express to someone else what you believe. But it cannot convince someone whose *etzem nekuda* lies elsewhere.
That is also why, whenever you come to something like this, as in Israel with the Jews and the Arabs, democracy does not work, because it is a religious thing.

sensitivity.reason: A political opinion on the conflict between Jews and Arabs in Israel and on democracy there.

blocks.text: Two people cannot be told to sit down and compromise when their inner goals conflict. On things that serve the goal they can: we want different things but find one to our mutual benefit, and both gain. On the goal itself there is no room, since one *etzem ratzon* is the exact opposite of the other.

But when the issue is the thing itself, one man's life against another's, compromise is impossible: "It's an all-or-nothing deal." So too within one person: of these essential wills he can really have only one at a time.

blocks.title: Totally nice, always
blocks.text: Some people live in *Tohu*, in the *igulim*. They lock on to *chesed* and resolve to be totally nice, always. Lacking a mature view, they do not see that to accomplish *chesed* you sometimes have to do something outwardly *gevura* (might, restraint), even when *chesed* is the real goal; that is the *inyan* of *Tikun*. So they try to be altruistically nice all the time, and get stepped on. Try it with a country, or a classroom: eventually it fails, and so it dies.

blocks.title: "Get it yourself"
blocks.text:
Then he switches to *gevura*, also in the way of *Tohu*: anyone who asks him to pass the salt is told, "Get it yourself." There is a *maala* (an advantage) in making people work, but giving everyone only what he deserves does not work either, and that too dies.

So with each of them: a person or a society that makes one the cure-all fails. And only one is possible at a time, because in essence they contradict each other.

phrases.he: (כמחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל וכהאי גוונא,
דגם שמנגדו יקשה עליו
phrases.en: even if the opposition will ask questions to him,

phrases.he: ולא יוכל למצוא טעם
phrases.en: and he's not able to find an explanation,

phrases.he: ישתוק,
phrases.en: he'll be quiet,

phrases.he: אבל לא יוכל להודות ולחזור בו,
phrases.en: he's not able to admit and then change his mind,

phrases.he: להתכלל בדעה שמנגדו כלל כו')
phrases.en: to the opposite opinion at all.

blocks.text: Like the dispute of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. Why did they not convince each other? They were reasonable people. Because their dispute came from an essential difference, from the root of their souls, not from *sechel*: a *Tohu* kind of thing. But they were in holiness, which is why this is in parentheses: it is not a full example.

Once the *halacha* (the law) was decided, Beis Shammai did like Beis Hillel, or the reverse, whichever way it went. Their essential leaning biased how they saw things, but their bond with Torah was deeper: if the Torah said to do it this way, they would, even without seeing it so.

So **even if the opposition will ask questions to him**, and **he's not able to find an explanation, he'll be quiet** and admit he does not know. But he cannot give up his opinion, because it does not rest on logic: he perceives things that way, and the *sechel* only looks for the words. That is how it works in Torah: they perceive it in spirituality, then look for words to bring it into human intellect, which is not its root.

But **he's not able to admit and then change his mind** and agree **to the opposite opinion at all**. Each holds a point that is essential, and *eilu v'eilu divrei Elokim chaim* ("these and these are the words of the living G-d"), so neither has reason to concede.

sections.title: Tikun: the midda spreads out of its essence, into a will for how to reach the goal
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the attribute comes out of its point: it is no longer about the goal but about how to accomplish it in a particular case. Then kindness depends on a reason, like kindness to one who did you a favor, and it is a composite kindness; so too the composite judgement of a kind man toward his enemy.

phrases.he: אבל בחינת התיקון היינו כאשר המדה בא מבחינת נקודה שלה להתפשטות חוץ מן העצמיות רצון ושכל שבה

blocks.text: *Tikun* is when the *midda* comes out of its point into *hispashtus*, outside its essence, will and intellect. Now we are not talking about your *etzem ratzon*, your goal; leave the goal aside. Now we are talking about how to accomplish it.

Your essential goal is the matter of religion. Religion is about ultimate truths, the ultimate reality and the ultimate goal of a person and of the world, so there can be only one truth: "you can't have pluralism in religion."

blocks.title: Going to New York by way of the south
blocks.text: The means are another matter. Traveling, you have to know your destination, and that you cannot change: going to New York, you are not going to Chicago; you have to pick. But sometimes, to go north, you have to go south, around something, and that is a separate *ratzon*. Whoever just starts walking straight toward it runs into all the walls in his way.

blocks.title: The short long way and the long short way
blocks.text: Like the story of the long short way and the short long way. A man wants to reach the palace. The straight road, the short long way, brings him very close, but a wall stands in front of him and he cannot get in: short, but long. The long short way compromises and goes slowly, but it is short, because you actually get there. "Shortcuts make for long delays": clever schemes in these things are not worth it.
So this is the *inyan* of *Tikun*: no longer the *etzem ratzon*, but the *ratzon* for how to accomplish it in a particular case.

phrases.he: דהיינו כמו מדת החסד כאשר יולד הרצון ושכל להטות כלפי חסד לזולתו
מצד שעשה לו טובה
phrases.en: You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.

phrases.he: ולא מצד בחינת עצם הטוב הבא בגלוי בהכרח מטבע הטוב שבעצמיות נפשו
אדרבה יוכל להיות אכזרי בטבע,
phrases.en: The person could be cruel naturally.

phrases.he: ולמי שחננו והצילו ממות
phrases.en: But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him and saved his life,

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא
ירצה להטיב,
phrases.en: for that person he's going to always be gracious,

phrases.he: ויטה שכלו עליו תמיד לחסד וזכות
phrases.en: and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably.

phrases.he: כו' וכהאי גוונא

blocks.text: For example *chesed*, when the will and intellect to be kind to another are born because he did you a favor. Not that in your essence you always want to be kind to everybody: **You want to be nice to somebody because he did you a favor.**

Say he wants his own happiness, or money. If a man helps him out, he will be kind to him, reasoning that it will help him more later; or he may simply be grateful by nature. But he does not act this way with everybody: he is nice to those who are nice to him, and not to those who are not.

It is not the essential kindness that comes necessarily from the good nature of his soul. Out of essential *chesed* he would have to be nice to everybody, whatever they had done to him, because that is his nature.

On the contrary, **the person could be cruel naturally**. **But to somebody that saved his life, that did a lot of kindness to him**, **he's going to always be gracious**, **and he's always going to be biased to look at them favorably**. He has tied his *etzem ratzon* to that person as far as the person did for him: the more kindness, the more connection. Now it gets complicated, when to be nice and when not. This is the *ratzon murkav* (the composite will).

phrases.he: שזה נקרא חסד וטוב המורכב,
phrases.en: this is called a complex or composite kindness and good.

phrases.he: ולא חסד פשוט ועצמי
phrases.en: it's not the same simple thing for everybody

phrases.he: שמצד הטבע כלל
וכהאי גוונא יובן בהיפוכו,
phrases.en: the same way with the opposite,

phrases.he: במדת הדין המורכב, להטות רצונו ושכלו כלפי חוב לשונאו שעשה לו רעה הרבה,
גם שבעצם טבעו הוא איש חסדן ורחמן כו'
phrases.en: even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person,

blocks.text: This is **a complex or composite kindness and good**, *chesed hamurkav*: it has many parts, and the situation has to be weighed. It is no simple, essential *chesed* coming from nature; **it's not the same simple thing for everybody**.

The same with its opposite, the composite attribute of judgement: bending his will and intellect against an enemy and hater who did him much harm. Someone very mean to him becomes his enemy. That does not make him cruel, **even if *b'etzem* he's a kind person**: by nature he likes to be kind, but he has to see that there are people one should not be nice to.

Had he made *chesed* his whole *metzius* (existence), he would be nice even if it got him killed, even if it bit him back. But at the *pnimiyus* (the inner side), even within *Tohu* there is the head, the inner will they come from; so *Tikun* has a higher *shoresh* (root).

blocks.title: The parent who wants to be loved
blocks.text: A parent who wants a loving relationship with his children is outwardly kind so that they will appreciate and love him back. He does what they will see as kind, which does not mean he really wants to be kind. Go deeper: the inner will to be kind is for their benefit, and whoever really wants that will do what outwardly looks like *gevura*, as the *sechel* decides.

sections.title: In the composite, opposites can live together: love and hate, Shaul, Shlomo and the Flood
sections.summary: Once the attributes are tied to a thing through a reason, one thing can be loved from one side and hated from another, and a middle is weighed out between them. So G-d punished and honored Shaul at once, was angry and joyful over Shlomo, and found in man's evil inclination both a reason to destroy and a reason to spare: in *Tikun*, in the actual world, nothing is pure.

phrases.he: ועל דרך זה יובן שיוכל להיות במורכב כמה מיני אופנים שונים
phrases.en: once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways

phrases.he: מאד, לפי אופן דבר שמורכב בו המדות
phrases.en: according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos*.

phrases.he: כמו אהבה ושנאה
התלויים בדבר
phrases.en: that are dependent on something,

phrases.he: כנזכר לעיל
הרי יוכל למצוא דבר שמצדו א' יאהבנו, ויהיה רצונו ושכלו הכל לטוב וחסד, ומצדו הב' באותו הדבר עצמו, ישנאנו ויטה רצונו ושכלו לרע ועונש

blocks.text: So the composite can come out in very different ways: **once you start having these considerations, it can come out in many different ways**, **according to the considerations that you're using to put together the *middos***. Like love and hate **that are dependent on something**: one and the same thing he can love from one side, with will and intellect for good and kindness, and hate from another, leaning to bad and punishment.
Once your essential *middos* hang on something through a *sechel*, it can be good for you by one consideration and bad by another: from this side you love it, from that side you hate it.

blocks.title: Drugs and their side effects
blocks.text: Drugs, for example. People like them because they feel good, and hate them for their side effects. They love the positive and hate the negative, but since it is one thing in the world, both are tied to it, and you cannot have one without the other.
With both tied to one thing, your *sechel* links two opposite *middos* to it, and you have to decide which wins in practice, and how to act.

phrases.he: עד שיוכל להיות בחינת ממוצע
phrases.en: until you come out with a *memutza*

phrases.he: כלול מחסד וגבורה יחד

blocks.text: Until there can be a *memutza* (a middle), including *chesed* and *gevura* together. Essentially nothing mixes: what you like you like totally, and what you hate you hate totally. But in practice you can prioritize, and place a thing somewhere in the middle of your list of things you like, good on one hand and bad on the other.

blocks.title: Profit and expenses in a business deal
blocks.text: But in an actual physical thing both come together, so you can do a simple equation: weigh the pleasure against the pain, subtract, and maximize. Like a business deal: you want the profit and not the expenses. A deal may bring in money but cost more than it gains, and is not worth it; or you gain a little; or a lot.

blocks.title: Only a deal that is profitable enough
blocks.text: The money coming back is always what you want. But acting by *sechel*, you take only a deal profitable enough to meet your needs, not just any deal that ends with somebody paying you. So you build a hierarchy, this better than that, and a *memutza*: this one is so-so.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב באשר משפטו שם כו'
על שאול שהמית את הגבעונים ועל שלא נספד כהלכה,
דבר והיפוכו כאחד

blocks.text: As it is written, *ba'asher mishpato sham* (he cannot recall the end of the word): where *Hashem* judges, there you find His compassion and His *chesed*. It seems like opposites.

blocks.title: Shaul punished and eulogized
blocks.text: This was said of Shaul, who killed the Givonim and was not properly eulogized: one thing and its opposite at once. Because Shaul had killed the Givonim, who had helped Dovid, a plague came; through prophecy they learned it was because of Shaul, and Dovid handed some of Shaul's descendants to the Givonim to be hanged. That was Shaul's punishment. At the same time Dovid was told to make a *hesped* (eulogy) for Shaul, since he had never been given proper honor.

So is G-d angry with Shaul or pleased with him? He punishes and rewards him at once. It was not essential, as if He simply hated Shaul or liked him. A parent who yells at a child for doing wrong still loves him: he likes the good the child does and not the bad. The two are not connected, so both can be at once.

phrases.he: וכן כשנשא שלמה בת פרעה,
phrases.en: also with *Shlomo*, that *Hashem* was angry because he married *Bas Paroh*,

phrases.he: על זה אמר כי על אפי כו'
phrases.en: that this is: I'm angry,

phrases.he: ושיר השירים נאמר על שמחת בנין בית המקדש
וכמו שכתוב ביום שמחת לבו כו'
phrases.en: the day of the rejoicing of his heart, which is the time the *Beis HaMikdash* was built,

phrases.he: שמחה וחרון אף, דבר והיפוכו כאחד
phrases.en: So we see that *Hashem* both had *simcha* and anger at *Shlomo* at the same time.

blocks.text: So too Shlomo. *Hashem* was angry that he married *Bas Paroh* (Pharaoh's daughter): *ki al api*, "**I'm angry**", angry forever. Yet *Shir HaShirim* (the Song of Songs) was said on the joy of building the *Beis HaMikdash* (the Temple), a song of *simcha* (joy) and of how much *Hashem* loved Shlomo, "on the day of the rejoicing of his heart," the day it was built. Joy and burning anger, at once.

phrases.he: וכן כי יצר לב האדם רע וכו'
phrases.en: and the same thing with man

phrases.he: ומתחלה אמר וירא יהו״ה כי רבה רעת האדם כו' וינחם כו'
phrases.en: First, before the flood, it says G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

blocks.text: And **the same thing with man**. Before the *Mabul* (the Flood) G-d said: since man is bad, we will destroy him. After it He said: since man is bad, we will not. The same fact, that man has a *yetzer hara* (evil inclination), was a reason both to hate him and to pity him.

blocks.title: Both sides of a court case
blocks.text: One side says that since men are bad they should be destroyed; the other, that they are born bad, so it is not their fault. It is like a court case, where each side shows how the same *nekuda* leads to *chesed* or to *gevura*: born bad means they will sin; born bad means go easy on them; no, born bad means there is no hope at all. It just depends: "Whatever you want, you'll be able to use that as an excuse for it."

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: In the end, before the *Mabul* the bad could not be refined; after it the world was refined a little, which is why there can be a rainbow. In a rainbow the cloud obstructs the light. Before, the atmosphere was too thick; after, it was thinner, so the light came through, struck the raindrops and made a rainbow, revealing the light's hidden beauty through that resistance.

blocks.title: Why the rainbow came after the Flood
blocks.text: So after the *Mabul* a person's bad was refined enough to be used for good: he can overcome his *yetzer hara*, and the fight itself, the difficulty of doing what G-d wants, brings out the inner beauty of his bond with G-d, of his *nefesh Elokis* (G-dly soul). Before the *Mabul* it could not be used that way, so the bad side won.
At first, before the *Mabul*, G-d saw how bad man was, and He regretted making man.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר
שזהו מבחינת המדות דתיקון,
phrases.en: the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun*,

phrases.he: שהם בבחינת מורכבים
phrases.en: which are complex.

phrases.he: דהיינו בהתפשטות דבר
phrases.en: that you're dealing not with a theory.

phrases.he: שלא מצד העצמיות לבד
על כן יוכל להיות התכללות דבר והיפוכו כו'
phrases.en: Therefore, you can have two opposite things,

blocks.text: As a *maamar* (discourse) explains, this belongs to the *middos* of *Tikun*: **the fact that you can have both *middos* for the same thing is because it's in *Tikun***, where they are composite, in the thing's *hispashtus*. In theory things can be pure; in practice nothing is. Everything has a benefit and a cost, and no physical thing is wholly pleasure or wholly pain.

blocks.title: All the powers of the soul in one body
blocks.text: In the *hispashtus*, the physical world, everything comes together, as when the soul enters the body: the body separates each power, yet sight, hearing and all the soul's powers meet in one body. So any physical thing holds all the *sefiros* and *middos* in one, in different proportions, and is never found as just itself.

blocks.title: No light without a little darkness
blocks.text: **Therefore, you can have two opposite things**, one thing and its opposite together. In theory light and darkness, or sweet and bitter, are complete opposites; in practice nothing is not a mixture of both. There is no light so pure that it could not be brighter, which means there is a little darkness in it.

sections.title: Tohu stays a sefira; only Tikun makes a partzuf, a person, like fire and water mixed
sections.summary: Even divided into ten, the point of *Tohu* is only a *sefira*, not the *partzuf* of a person who includes all opposites. A person, and *Tikun*, sees the deeper goal both sides share and works it out in practice, without dropping the goal; as *Sefer Yetzira* says, G-d mixed fire and water, not in their essence but as composites.

phrases.he: והיינו בחינת נקודה דתהו,
דגם כשנעשה בהתחלקות לי', אין זה רק ספירה
phrases.en: Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos*.

blocks.text: This is the point of *Tohu*, the essential *middos*: *Akudim*, one point. **Even in *Tohu*, when it divides up into a *sefira*, and it has ten *sefiros*, they're also *nekudos***, so it is not real *hiskalelus*. In *Tohu* the *gevura* is all *chesed*, one *sefira*: the *chesed* takes the *gevura* and makes it *chesed* too.

blocks.title: Even more reason to be nice to him
blocks.text: Like those who lean towards *chesed*: tell them how bad a man is and all the bad he did, and they find in it even more reason to be nice to him, the poor victim. They turn anything into a *chesed*.

Because it is a *sefira*: a man who in his essence believes or wants a certain way, from his *emuna* (faith) or his will. He may come and talk to you on purpose, even go out to missionize, like the *Akudim* of *Tohu*; but it is still one *sefira*, and he is not considering the other side at all.

You see the sign of it a lot. A person in the way of *Tohu* tries to make his whole *partzuf* of one *sefira*. But the real *etzem* includes all ten, and he should be able to hold them together. One who cannot shows a great *shtarkeit* (fierceness), a fierce opposition to the opposite, because he feels it threatens his *inyan*.

*Tikun* needs a deeper look; the next chapter explains the middle *kav* (line), which joins opposites. Take two opposite opinions: the *chesed* man fiercely opposes the *gevura* side, the *gevura* man the *chesed* view, and each sees the other as "completely evil and wrong and subversive."

But a *bar daas* (a person of *daas*), as the Frierdiker Rebbe (the previous Lubavitcher Rebbe) describes *daas* (knowledge) in a *maamar*, takes the two and offers to explain each one's view to him better than he understands it himself. He peels it down to the real depth: you do not really want a particular instance of *chesed*. He shows them the real *etzem ratzon* of *chesed*, before it is tied to a deed, and brings it up a step.

Up a step, you ask why you really want *chesed*, and what the theory behind it is. Every person has a little good in him, and you lean towards letting him off because you value that good and want to bring it out and see it expressed. That is the main *nekuda*, and brought out, it will help him and others.

*Gevura* answers that what is inside does not matter, good intentions or potential; if it does not come out in deed, it is worthless. So the *bar daas* tells them that they both want the same thing: that the inner good come out and be expressed. Now they have to decide the best way to get this person to bring out his inner good.

By telling him he is really good, that we love him and value him as a person? Or by being strict, telling him he is not doing well enough and we expect more? It depends on the person and his nature. So you will do whichever it takes: for your real goal it does not matter which you do, only which works.

blocks.title: Live and let live, or sit down together
blocks.text: To bring the *middos* of *Tohu* truly into *Tikun*: there is a *Tikun* after a *midda* of *Tohu* that is like a *reshus harabim* (a public domain), something like America. Everyone keeps his own *ratzon* and its opposites; we only see to it that people do not kill those with opposite views, and they deal with each other in things that do not touch their essential will.

But a real *Tikun* means two people actually sit down and work together. For that you have to find their real, deeper goal, one that transcends both their particulars. In *Tohu*, though, even when it comes out, it becomes only a *sefira*, not a *partzuf*.

phrases.he: ולא פרצוף אדם,
phrases.en: It's not a person.

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההתכללות מכל ההפכים כו'

blocks.text: Not the *partzuf* of a person. It is not a person; you are still talking to a wall. The *inyan* of a person is the inclusion of all opposites.

You see this a lot with *baalei teshuva* (returnees to Judaism). Without proper instruction it is very easy for them to end up not being a person. Their whole approach to religion is *emuna*, with a passionate drive for altruism; tied to one aspect of the truth, it makes them forcefully attached to it, and they are not going to be human. There is no sitting down and talking with them: they are on a holy mission, and when you try to talk to them, they are not there.

sensitivity.reason: A generalisation about baalei teshuva: that without proper instruction they easily end up "not human", impossible to talk to.
sensitivity.publishable: You see this a lot. Without proper instruction it is very easy for a person to end up not being a person. If his whole approach to religion is *emuna*, with a passionate drive for altruism, tied to one aspect of the truth, it makes him forcefully attached to it, and he is not going to be human. There is no sitting down and talking with him: he is on a holy mission, and when you try to talk to him, he is not there.

blocks.text: Say something they do not want to hear and they get angry and try to put you down, even insult you, to invalidate your opinion, whether by invalidating you or the thing itself. They already know it is bad, so it does not matter how they take it away from you; they are not weighing what you say. It is not healthy, and not comfortable to be around.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the generalisation about baalei teshuva who were not properly instructed.
sensitivity.publishable: Say something he does not want to hear and he gets angry and tries to put you down, even insult you, to invalidate your opinion, whether by invalidating you or the thing itself. He already knows it is bad, so it does not matter how he takes it away from you; he is not weighing what you say. It is not healthy, and not comfortable to be around.

blocks.text: So that is not a person. A person sees a deeper will and how all these *ratzonos* fit together, and so can see the other's view: by a *ratzon murkav* I may think this is better in practice, but I understand him, and I have a will for that too.
Like the Baal Shem Tov's saying: if you see a bad in somebody else, you have it in yourself. Whatever you see in another you have in some way; every person really has all these *ratzonos*.

blocks.title: The truth, and the lower realms
blocks.text: Often people fight because they lock onto two essential wills when inwardly they want the same thing. Take *emuna* and making a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below): taking the full truth of *Yiddishkeit* and bringing it down into the world, the lower realms. One locks onto the first half, that the truth cannot be diluted if it is to be a *dira b'tachtonim*; the other onto its having to be in the lower realms.

It is like one person in the lights and vessels of *Tohu*, another in those of *Tikun*. One drops the real goal just to compromise; another keeps his goal but will never reach it, because he will not compromise on how. Some are very altruistic but not practical, some practical. Your real goal is to bring it out, so you need both.

phrases.he: אלא בבחינת התיקון, דוקא
phrases.en: the *inyan* of a person is *davka* in a way of *Tikun*,

phrases.he: שכל נקודה בא בהתפשטות חוץ מעצמיותה,
שאז מתכללים על ידי ריבוי הכלים מכלים שונים שמורכבים בהם כו'
phrases.en: when it comes out from the *etzem hanekuda* into *Tikun*, then all the opposite things are expressed, but they're expressed in a limited way, kind of.

phrases.he: ודי למבין

blocks.title: From the yeshiva to mivtzaim
blocks.text: Rather, only in *Tikun*, when every *nekuda* comes out into *hispashtus*, outside its essence: **the *inyan* of a person is *davka* in a way of *Tikun***. You do not leave the *nekuda* in its altruism. A teenager sitting in *yeshiva* can easily be altruistic; out on *mivtzaim* (outreach) you have to be practical. You cannot tell someone you want to bring closer that religion is all or nothing, that believing in Judaism means doing everything it says. That is really the truth: if this is what G-d wants, I will do everything. But in practice, a person cannot start by doing everything.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 opens with the first half of line 46 (w0-59), read without the alignment's mark, which falls on the second half at w1201.

blocks.text: It is the same *mashal* we used for the *igulim*: they are the thing in hiddenness, and this is the thing revealed in a particular. They correspond; the only difference is whether it is the essence or already for a particular.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: That is what a person needs to bring it into *Tikun*, to make *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent). He does not drop the essential thing; he writes it on a piece of paper, puts it in his pocket, and asks what his practical goal is. If he really wants what *Hashem* wants, a baby step he can actually take is not hypocritical: it is the only way he will ever get there.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: The *yetzer hara* gets a person to insist on doing everything, and doing it right, perfectly, or not at all. Why the *yetzer hara*? Because it comes from *Tohu*, from all or nothing.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: From the *chesed* of *Tohu* one says: I have an essential bond with G-d, He will be with me and love me whatever I do, so it does not matter what I do. That can come out as *kelipa* (what conceals G-dliness): the *chesed* of *Tohu* becomes the root of the *kelipa* of Yishmael.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: The *gevura* of *Tohu* says that nothing one does will ever be good enough for G-d: never doing the *mitzvos* perfectly, never expressing in action the full glory He deserves, for "there is no righteous man on earth." And if one will never be perfect and there is always room to improve, what is the point of starting?
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And this is the root of the *kelipa* of Esav, a *gevura* of *kelipa*. He does not know much about Muslim philosophy, but this is what Christianity says: G-d wants you to do the Torah and the *mitzvos*, but you cannot do them without sinning, without messing up somewhere, so you need not do any of them; just rely on being saved by "Yoshke". So out of the *gevura* of *kelipa* came a kind of *chesed*, that you can really do whatever you want. They are so *gevura*-dik by nature that they give up.

sensitivity.reason: Describes Christian teaching on the commandments disparagingly and names its founder with a derogatory Yiddish nickname.

One says: G-d wants you to do the Torah and the *mitzvos*, but you cannot do them without sinning, without messing up somewhere, so you need not do any of them. So out of the *gevura* of *kelipa* came a kind of *chesed*, that you can really do whatever you want. Such people are so *gevura*-dik by nature that they give up.

blocks.text: This is what the *yetzer hara* does: it makes a person altruistic, after a fashion, locked into one essential *midda* until it is debilitating and he does nothing. That is a *ratzo* (running towards) without a *shov* (returning): a *ratzo* for the *Tohu*, which is good, with no focus on the result.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: Focused on the result, wanting it to come down in practice, you ask how this *chesed* can move you to do good: however low I am, there is always some meaningful step I can take, and I have value. A person feels lifted: G-d treasures him, and his small effort is worth as much to G-d as a great *tzaddik*'s (righteous person's), because it is on his level. That is how it comes into holiness.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: And the *gevura* side: however much I have done, I can never rest content, because there is always room to improve. That is how Yitzchak and Yaakov used *chesed* and *gevura*. The difference is whether you are focused on the bottom line, what you actually accomplish. If so, it is of *Tikun*, a good thing; if not, it is *Tohu*.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 76 speaks on line 46 from its opening reading of the line's first half (w0-59) until it reads the second half at w1201, where the alignment marks the line.

blocks.text: Then they are revealed through the many vessels compounded in them: **when it comes out from the *etzem hanekuda* into *Tikun*, then all the opposite things are expressed, but they're expressed in a limited way, kind of**. Each finds its place. That is a *partzuf*: all are expressed together because each is limited to one instance.

phrases.he: וזה מה שכתוב בספר יצירה
טרף אש ומים ובללן זה בזה
phrases.en: Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together.

phrases.he: דהיינו בחינת המורכב דאש ומים דוקא, ולא בעצם מהותן כו' וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות:

blocks.text: And this is what *Sefer Yetzira* (the Book of Formation) says: **Take *eish u'mayim* and mix them together**; that is how *Hashem* made the world. Essential fire and essential water are opposites, physically and spiritually, but a physical world needed those forms combined. No physical thing is purely fire or purely water, and so too spiritually.

That is, the composite of fire and water *davka* (specifically), not their very essence, as explained elsewhere at length. In physical things one never comes without the other: nothing is outwardly perfect, and nothing is without merit. You always have both.

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that each *sefira* of *Tohu* is a *nekuda*, and why does dividing each *sefira* into ten make *Tikun*?
Why is the person who reads Dale Carnegie's book not *chafetz chesed*, and what does the essential will for kindness have that his will lacks?
Why can two opposite essential wills not compromise, and what happens to the person who is "totally nice, always" or who says "get it yourself"?
Why could Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel not convince each other, and why is their dispute only half an example?
How is kindness to one who saved your life different from the kindness of a person who is kind by nature?
How could G-d punish Shaul and order his eulogy at the same time, and what does that show about the composite *middos* of *Tikun*?

In the verses (Shmuel II 21) the plague is for Shaul's killing of the Givonim; the link to helping Dovid comes through the city of Nov, whose kohanim gave Dovid food and whom the Givonim served (a Midrashic reading). The block keeps his words; a reviewer may want to check.
"Where His judgement is, there..." (74 w1106): he says he forgets the end of the verse; the block keeps it as an unfinished quotation.

"That's the way that Yitzchak and Yaakov used chesed and gevura" (76 w1138-1150): kept as he said it, though chesed and gevura are usually paired with Avraham and Yitzchak. A reviewer may want to check whether he misspoke. The next sentence's "the ratzui of Tikun" (76 w1173-1185) is unclear in the transcript and is rendered only as "it is of Tikun".

"The long short way and the short long way" (73 w1638-1776): he tells it without naming the source; it is the Gemara's story (Eruvin 53b) of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and a child at a crossroads, which he retells as a way to a palace. Kept as he tells it.
